s: On July 20, 1969, Apollo 11 landed on the Moon.
Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin spent about two and a half hours walking on the lunar surface.
They planted an American flag
and took a live phone call from President Nixon.
Millions of people watched the landing on television,
many of them in crystal-clear high definition.
w: Television in 1969 was grainy, low-resolution analogue video — the moonwalk footage is famously fuzzy. High-definition broadcasts didn’t reach homes until the late 1990s and 2000s.

s: The Declaration of Independence was adopted in Philadelphia on July 4, 1776.
Thomas Jefferson was its principal author.
It was printed on paper and read aloud to crowds.
Word of it crossed the Atlantic as fast as it could,
flashed to London by electric telegraph within hours.
w: The electric telegraph wasn’t invented until the 1830s–40s. News of the Declaration took weeks to reach England — carried, like everything else, by sailing ship.

s: The Great Fire of London broke out in a bakery on Pudding Lane in September 1666.
It raged for four days and destroyed much of the medieval City of London.
Tens of thousands of Londoners fled with whatever they could carry.
Firefighters fought the blaze with buckets, axes, and firehooks.
Steam-powered fire engines finally pumped water from the Thames to stop it.
w: Steam fire engines are a 19th-century invention. The Great Fire was finally stopped the old way — by blowing up houses with gunpowder to create firebreaks.

s: Orville and Wilbur Wright made the first powered airplane flight at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, on December 17, 1903.
The flight was also filmed with a movie camera for the newsreels.
The first flight lasted 12 seconds and covered about 120 feet.
A single still photograph captured the moment of liftoff.
It was taken by rescue crewman John T. Daniels,
who had never used a camera before that day.
w: No film of the first flight exists — only the famous still photograph, snapped by lifesaver John T. Daniels, who had indeed never handled a camera before.

s: Around the year 1000, Norse explorers led by Leif Erikson reached North America,
sailing west from Greenland.
They built a small settlement at a place they called Vinland, in what is now Newfoundland.
The sagas say they clashed with the local people they called Skraelings.
The Norse explored the coastline on horseback.
w: There were no horses in the Americas — they had gone extinct there thousands of years earlier and were only reintroduced by Spanish ships after 1492.

s: The RMS Titanic sank on her maiden voyage in April 1912 after striking an iceberg.
Her wireless operators sent distress calls by radio to nearby ships.
They also emailed the White Star Line’s New York office for help.
More than 2,200 people were aboard, and over 1,500 died.
The Carpathia answered the call and rescued over 700 survivors.
w: Email didn’t exist in 1912. Wireless (radio) telegraphy was the only instant long-distance link a ship had — which is exactly why Titanic’s operators used it.

s: The Rosetta Stone was carved in Egypt in 196 BCE during the Ptolemaic dynasty.
It records a decree issued at Memphis.
The text appears in three scripts: Greek, Latin, and Egyptian hieroglyphs.
Scholars who could read Greek used the stone to crack the hieroglyphic code.
Jean-François Champollion announced the decipherment in 1822.
w: The three scripts are Greek, Egyptian hieroglyphs, and Demotic — the everyday script of Egypt. Latin appears nowhere on the stone.

s: The Black Death reached Europe in 1347 aboard Genoese merchant ships.
Within five years it killed perhaps a third of the continent’s population.
The plague raced between ports faster than any epidemic before it, carried by steamship.
Flagellants marched between towns, and public prayers were held for relief.
Some towns drove away travelers to keep the plague out.
w: Steamships belong to the 19th century. The medieval plague moved at the speed of sailing ships, carts, and travelers on foot.

s: Johannes Gutenberg perfected his movable-type printing press in Mainz around 1440.
His 42-line Bible, finished in the 1450s, was printed on vellum shipped from the Americas.
Around 180 copies were produced.
Most were printed on paper made from linen rags.
Gutenberg’s press transformed Europe within decades.
w: Nothing was shipped from the Americas in the 1450s — Europeans didn’t know the continent existed until 1492. The Bible’s paper came from Italian and German mills; some copies are on vellum, but European vellum.

s: Napoleon was defeated at Waterloo in June 1815.
He surrendered to the British and was exiled to Saint Helena in the South Atlantic.
In quiet moments at Longwood House he typed out passages of his memoir on a typewriter.
For the most part, he dictated to companions.
He died there in 1821.
w: Practical typewriters only appeared in the 1860s–70s, decades after Napoleon’s death. He dictated his memoirs; his companions wrote with pen and ink.

s: The first modern Olympic Games opened in Athens in April 1896.
Athletes from 14 nations competed in the Panathenaic Stadium.
American James Connolly won the first event, the triple jump.
Greek runner Spyridon Louis’s marathon victory made him a national hero.
The opening ceremony was broadcast live on Greek radio.
w: Radio broadcasting began in the 1920s, decades later. In 1896 the results traveled by newspaper, telegraph, and word of mouth.

s: Abraham Lincoln delivered the Gettysburg Address on November 19, 1863, at the dedication of a soldiers’ cemetery.
His speech ran about two minutes,
after a two-hour oration by Edward Everett.
Newspapers printed the text, and it quickly became famous.
A clear audio recording of the address survives in the Library of Congress.
w: No recording of Lincoln exists — the phonograph wasn’t invented until 1877, fourteen years later. We know the address only through newspapers and written copies.

s: King John sealed the Magna Carta at Runnymede in June 1215.
The charter limited royal power over the church, the barons, and free men.
Scribes wrote each copy out by hand, in ink on parchment.
Copies were run off on a printing press and sent to every English county.
About a dozen originals still survive today.
w: The printing press didn’t reach Europe until the 1440s. Every Magna Carta copy was written by hand — which is why only about a dozen survive.

s: On the night of November 9, 1989, border guards stood aside and crowds crossed freely.
The Wall had divided East and West Berlin for 28 years.
Celebrants chipped pieces off the concrete as souvenirs.
East and West Berliners compared notes on social media that night.
The fall of the Wall led to German reunification within a year.
w: Social networks like Facebook and Twitter were still years away in 1989. Berliners swapped stories face to face, and watched state TV — some of which had stopped taking orders.

s: Leonardo da Vinci began painting the Mona Lisa in Florence in the early 1500s.
He carried the portrait with him to France, where he died in 1519.
He had studied the sitter’s shifting expressions through a telescope he built.
The painting later entered the French royal collection,
and it now hangs in the Louvre behind protective glass.
w: The telescope wasn’t invented until 1608, nearly a century after Leonardo. The smile’s mystery comes from his sfumato technique — soft, blurred edges — not from any optical device.

s: Archduke Franz Ferdinand of Austria was assassinated in Sarajevo on June 28, 1914.
The assassin, Gavrilo Princip, was a 19-year-old Bosnian Serb.
Breaking-news alerts about the assassination flashed on television screens across Europe that evening.
The killing set off a chain reaction of alliances that became the First World War.
Within weeks, all the great powers were at war.
w: Television broadcasting didn’t begin until the 1920s–30s. In 1914 the news moved by telegraph wire and morning newspapers.

s: On June 6, 1944, Allied forces landed on five beaches in Normandy.
General Eisenhower coordinated the operation from Portsmouth by satellite phone.
It was the largest seaborne invasion in history.
Paratroopers dropped behind enemy lines before dawn.
By the end of August, Allied armies had liberated Paris.
w: The first satellites weren’t launched until 1957. D-Day was coordinated by radio, telephone lines, and officers carrying orders by hand and boat.

s: The Soviet Union launched Sputnik 1, the first artificial satellite, on October 4, 1957.
Backyard observers plotted its orbit with GPS receivers.
Its beeps were picked up by amateur radio operators around the world.
The launch shocked America and set off the Space Race.
Sputnik burned up in the atmosphere the following January.
w: GPS wasn’t operational until the 1990s. Cold War amateurs tracked Sputnik the analog way — radio direction-finding, radar, and the naked eye.

s: Constantinople fell to Sultan Mehmed II’s Ottoman army on May 29, 1453.
The city’s Theodosian Walls had held for over a thousand years.
News of the fall ran in printed newspapers across Europe within days.
A 53-day siege and the Ottomans’ great bombards finally breached the walls.
Emperor Constantine XI died in the final assault.
w: Printed newspapers first appeared in the early 1600s — Gutenberg’s press was barely a decade old in 1453. The news traveled by letters and travelers’ reports, over weeks.

s: Queen Victoria reigned from 1837 to 1901 — 63 years and 216 days.
For her Diamond Jubilee in 1897, troops from across the Empire paraded through London.
The jubilee procession was broadcast live on television to celebrating crowds.
Her reign had spanned the rise of railways, telegraph, and photography.
It was the first Diamond Jubilee ever celebrated by a British monarch.
w: Regular television broadcasting began in 1936, long after Victoria’s death in 1901. The 1897 crowds watched the procession in person; everyone else read about it.

s: Isaac Newton’s Principia Mathematica was published in 1687.
Edmond Halley — of comet fame — paid for the printing out of his own pocket.
The book laid out the laws of motion and universal gravitation.
It transformed physics, though it sold few copies at first.
Newton promoted the book with an interview on a popular science podcast.
w: Podcasts are a 21st-century medium; in 1687 nothing on Earth could even record a voice. Newton’s circle discussed the book in letters and at Royal Society meetings.

s: On the night of December 16, 1773, colonists dumped 342 chests of tea into Boston Harbor.
Some of the chests also held green tea imported from Japan.
Most of the destroyed tea was black Bohea tea shipped from China.
The protesters were angry about a British tax on tea.
The stunt pushed the colonies and Britain toward revolution.
w: The East India Company’s tea was Chinese — Japan was closed to Western trade at the time. No Japanese tea appears anywhere in the cargo lists.

t: Great Pyramid of Giza · c. 2560 BCE
s: The Great Pyramid of Giza was built around 2560 BCE for the pharaoh Khufu.
It was the tallest man-made structure on Earth for more than 3,800 years.
It is the only surviving wonder of the ancient world.
Its blocks were cut with copper and stone tools and hauled on wooden sledges.
The builders also used iron chisels and camel-drawn carts.
w: The Iron Age hadn’t reached Egypt, and camels weren’t pack animals there until many centuries later. Copper tools, sledges, ramps, and human muscle built it.

s: Charles Lindbergh flew solo from New York to Paris in May 1927 aboard the Spirit of St. Louis.
The flight took about 33 and a half hours.
Over the open Atlantic he followed GPS waypoints.
He fought fog, ice, and exhaustion for more than a day in the air.
He landed at Le Bourget to a cheering crowd of thousands.
w: GPS wasn’t operational until decades later. Lindbergh navigated the old way — compass, dead reckoning, and occasional stars.

s: Cleopatra VII was Egypt’s last active pharaoh, ruling until 30 BCE.
She was of Macedonian Greek descent,
the heir of one of Alexander the Great’s generals.
She met both Julius Caesar and Mark Antony in person.
She lived closer in time to the building of the Great Pyramid than to the invention of the smartphone.
w: It’s the other way around — and it’s the best fact in history: the pyramid was already about 2,500 years old in her time, while the smartphone came only about 2,000 years later. Cleopatra is closer to the iPhone than to Khufu.

s: During the Second World War, codebreakers at Bletchley Park cracked Germany’s Enigma cipher.
They published bestselling memoirs about it immediately after the war.
Alan Turing helped design the Bombe machine that sped up the daily codebreaking.
Their work is widely credited with shortening the war.
Churchill called them “the geese that laid the golden eggs — and never cackled.”
w: Bletchley stayed secret until the 1970s — veterans couldn’t even tell their families what they’d done. The story only broke with F. W. Winterbotham’s The Ultra Secret in 1974.

s: Steve Jobs unveiled the iPhone in January 2007, and it went on sale that June.
It combined a phone, an iPod, and an internet communicator in one device.
Its 5-megapixel camera could record video.
It was controlled entirely with finger touches on a glass screen — no stylus.
Apple sold its millionth iPhone before the end of summer 2007.
w: The original iPhone had a 2-megapixel still camera and could not record video — video recording arrived with the iPhone 3GS in 2009.

s: Julius Caesar was stabbed to death in the Theatre of Pompey on the Ides of March, 44 BCE.
Weeks earlier he had been named dictator perpetuo — dictator for life.
His dying words, “Et tu, Brute?”, were written down by a scribe standing beside him.
Around 60 senators joined the plot.
His death set Rome on the road to civil war, and then to empire.
w: No ancient source records those words — Suetonius says Caesar said nothing. The line was invented by Shakespeare, over 1,600 years later.

s: Beethoven’s Fifth Symphony premiered in Vienna in December 1808.
The earliest recording of the symphony was captured that night on a wax cylinder.
The concert, in an unheated theater, ran more than four hours.
By then the composer’s hearing was seriously failing.
The Fifth went on to become the most famous symphony ever written.
w: The phonograph and wax cylinder weren’t invented until 1877, seven decades later. The premiere — famously chaotic — exists only in written accounts.

s: The 19th Amendment, giving American women the right to vote, was ratified on August 18, 1920.
It capped a 72-year campaign that began at Seneca Falls in 1848.
Susan B. Anthony lived to cast a legal ballot under the new amendment.
She had been arrested for voting illegally back in 1872.
The amendment is often called the “Anthony Amendment” in her honor.
w: Anthony died in 1906 — fourteen years before ratification. Her 1872 ballot was illegal; she never got to vote legally.

s: The Mona Lisa was stolen from the Louvre in August 1911 by Vincenzo Peruggia, an Italian handyman.
He hid in the museum overnight and walked out with the painting under his white smock.
Pablo Picasso was even questioned by police during the investigation.
The theft made the painting a household name.
Peruggia made his escape by helicopter from the museum’s courtyard.
w: Practical helicopters didn’t exist until 1936 — and Peruggia simply walked out, caught a train, and kept the painting in a trunk for two years.

s: The ancient Olympic Games began at Olympia in 776 BCE as a festival honoring Zeus.
Married women were welcome to compete alongside the men.
Champions received wreaths of wild olive leaves as their only prize.
Athletes competed nude in most events.
A separate festival, the Heraean Games, was held for unmarried girls.
w: Married women couldn’t even watch the Olympics — only the priestess of Demeter could sit in the stands. The Heraean Games were for unmarried girls only.

s: Every costume Viking wears horns, and the movies have taught generations to expect them.
The image has roots in the real thing: horned helmets do turn up in Viking graves, just rarely.
The stage gave the idea its grip: Carl Emil Doepler drew horned helmets for Wagner’s Ring at Bayreuth in 1876.
Before that production, illustrated Vikings rarely wore horns at all.
Bayreuth made the horns famous, and a century of cartoons has never let them go.
w: No horned Viking helmet has ever been found, rarely or otherwise. The horned look comes from Carl Emil Doepler’s 1876 costume designs for Wagner’s Ring cycle, and it has been stuck to Norse heads ever since.

s: Napoleon Bonaparte was a tiny man, barely five feet tall, and the soldiers nicknamed him for it.
The measurement is usually traced to his death, recorded at five foot two in the French inches of the day.
A French inch ran longer than an English inch, so the same height reads about five foot seven on an English ruler.
James Gillray and other British caricaturists had spent years drawing him as a squalling dwarf, so the math landed on ready ears.
Among his own officers he was middling height, short only beside the tall old guard he liked to stand beside.
w: The autopsy figure of five foot two was in French units, which makes him about five foot seven in English measure, average for his era. Gillray’s caricatures did the rest.

s: The story says young Albert Einstein failed mathematics and then rewrote physics anyway, which is why struggling students love him.
And the legend comes with paperwork: his school records are said to show him flunking mathematics, year after year.
The surviving report cards say the opposite: strong marks in mathematics at Munich, and again at Aarau in Switzerland.
He had mastered calculus by about fifteen, and at sixteen he failed only the Zurich Polytechnic entrance exam, on the non-math subjects.
One thread of the myth traces to Swiss grading, where 6 was the top mark, which a hasty reader could easily flip.
w: Einstein never failed math. He was fluent in calculus by fifteen, and his one famous stumble was the non-math sections of a polytechnic entrance exam at sixteen. The rest is legend.

s: In the summer of 64, fire broke out near the Circus Maximus and ran through Rome for the better part of a week.
A rumor spread that the emperor had set it himself, to clear ground for a golden palace.
Nero was thirty miles away at Antium when the first flames appeared, by the account of Tacitus.
Still, the story goes, he hurried back to Rome, took up his fiddle, and played while the city burned.
What is recorded is relief: he opened the Campus Martius and his own gardens to the crowds left homeless.
w: No fiddle existed in first-century Rome; bowed instruments would not arrive for another fifteen centuries. Tacitus reports Nero was away at Antium when the fire began, and that even the singing story was already called rumor.

s: The Great Wall of China threads thousands of miles across the north of the country, and schoolbooks love one claim about it.
The claim says it is the only human-made structure visible from space, and it predates spaceflight by decades.
A cartoonist’s column of the 1930s is usually credited with starting it.
Astronauts later confirmed the schoolbook claim word for word: from the Moon, the wall is plain to the naked eye.
The real reports run the other way: from orbit the wall is hard to pick out unaided, and from the Moon it is invisible.
w: No one has seen the wall from the Moon, and astronauts have struggled to spot it even from orbit without help. The claim goes back to a Ripley’s Believe It or Not cartoon in the 1930s, printed years before anyone had flown anywhere.

s: In 1692, the Massachusetts town of Salem executed twenty people for witchcraft in a summer of fear.
The condemned were burned at the stake, as the old law required, and the whole town turned out to watch the fires.
Nineteen were hanged on Gallows Hill, and one very stubborn man was pressed to death under stones for refusing to enter a plea.
Giles Corey’s death was the only one of its kind in the whole affair.
Burnings belonged to continental Europe; English law, which Massachusetts followed, sent witches to the gallows.
w: No one was burned at Salem. Nineteen were hanged, and Giles Corey was pressed to death for refusing to plead. The bonfires belong to Europe, not Massachusetts Bay.

s: When told that her starving subjects had no bread, the queen of France is said to have shrugged and answered with the most famous recipe in history.
The line is usually given as let them eat cake.
Her own letters confirm she said it, laughing, as the bread riots spread through Paris.
The phrase was already old when the future queen was a child: Rousseau wrote it down in the 1760s, crediting a nameless great princess.
The slander stuck because it fit the caricature, and it has been hers for two centuries.
w: No source ties the line to Marie Antoinette, who was still a child in Vienna when Rousseau first published it about a nameless princess. The attribution was too useful to die.

s: In 1492, Columbus sailed west across the Atlantic, and the story of his voyage usually comes with a subplot.
In the subplot, his own sailors feared tumbling off the edge of a flat world that only he believed was round.
His voyage is remembered as the moment Europe finally accepted the planet’s true shape.
Every educated European of his day already knew the world was round; the Greeks had measured its size seventeen centuries earlier.
The real argument was about distance: his critics thought Asia too far to reach westward, and they were right.
w: Nobody educated in 1492 believed the Earth was flat. Eratosthenes had measured its circumference by the third century BCE. The flat-earth subplot was invented by Washington Irving in the 1820s, and textbooks have been mopping up ever since.

s: Philadelphia ordered a bell for its State House in 1751 from the Whitechapel foundry in London.
It cracked on its first test ring, and the city had it recast twice by local founders.
The name comes not from independence but from abolitionists, who spread the bell’s inscription in the 1830s.
On July 4, 1776, its peal announced independence to the crowds gathered outside.
The famous big crack opened in 1846, while the bell tolled for George Washington’s birthday.
It was never rung again after that crack, and it later went on tour by rail to mend a divided country.
It now draws more than a million visitors a year, a short walk from Independence Hall.
w: There is no evidence the bell rang on July 4, 1776. The story traces to an 1847 work of fiction by George Lippard, and the State House steeple was in no shape for ringing that summer. The abolitionist christening, the 1846 crack, and the rest are documented.

s: George Washington suffered from terrible teeth his whole adult life.
By his first inauguration in 1789, exactly one natural tooth remained.
His famous dentures were carved from wood.
One surviving set includes human teeth, which his own account book shows were bought, not given.
The plates pinched and shifted, which changed the set of his face in later portraits.
He owned several sets over the years, no two alike, as his mouth kept changing.
John Greenwood, a New York dentist, made the later sets and tended them through the presidency.
The last surviving set is displayed at his estate at Mount Vernon.
w: Not wood. The surviving dentures are hippopotamus ivory, human teeth, and brass, mounted on lead. The wooden-teeth story was invented after his death and stuck because it made the great man sound folksy. His ledgers even record buying teeth from poor New Yorkers, a grim trade of the era.

s: In September 1519, five ships and about 270 men sailed from Spain under Ferdinand Magellan.
After a winter on the South American coast, the fleet found the strait that now bears his name.
Magellan himself completed the circumnavigation and returned to Spain in triumph.
He died in April 1521 at Mactan in the Philippines, killed in a local dispute he had no business joining.
Juan Sebastián Elcano brought the last ship, the Victoria, home in September 1522.
Aboard were eighteen starving men of the roughly 270 who had set out.
The cloves in the hold sold for just enough to pay for the whole venture.
w: Magellan never made it home. He fell at Mactan on April 27, 1521, and it was Elcano who completed the voyage with 18 men. It took three years, five ships, and nearly every life aboard; the spice cargo barely balanced the ledgers.

s: The gunfight at the O.K. Corral lasted about thirty seconds and left three men dead.
Dodge City at its wildest recorded a handful of killings in a bad year.
The frontier averaged a fatal shootout every week in every cow town.
Bank robbery was so rare that historians count fewer than a dozen across the whole frontier era.
What actually killed settlers was disease, drowning, and horses.
The famous Tombstone fight pitted lawmen against a cattle-rustling faction, not two lone gunslingers.
Dime novels and early Hollywood did most of the exaggerating.
w: No cow town saw weekly shootouts. Cattle-town homicide ran lower than in Eastern cities, and bank and stagecoach robberies barely register in the records. Dime novels arrived before the historians did, and the West has been paying for it ever since.

s: Mussolini’s regime is remembered around the world by one warm phrase: he made the trains run on time.
The line spread through the regime’s propaganda and through admirers abroad.
The state railways published punctuality figures that proved the miracle.
Italian railways had been overhauled during the First World War, years before the March on Rome.
No statistic from the era has ever surfaced to back the claim up.
What the trains ran on by 1943 was luck, with the fleet bombed and the rails torn up.
The phrase outlived both the regime and the man, proof that a slogan repeated often enough becomes history.
w: The punctuality figures do not exist. No record from Mussolini’s railways shows a turnaround, and the overhaul was underway before 1922. The line was propaganda that foreign admirers repeated as fact, and it worked so well it is quoted to this day.

s: On January 1, 1863, President Lincoln signed the Emancipation Proclamation.
It declared free every enslaved person in the United States, all at once.
On paper it reached some three and a half million people held in the rebelling states.
Union officers read it aloud wherever the army stood, from Virginia to the Mississippi.
Kentucky, Maryland, and Missouri stayed loyal to the Union and kept their own laws.
The proclamation also invited freedmen into uniform, and nearly 200,000 eventually served.
The Thirteenth Amendment finished the work in December 1865.
w: The proclamation applied only to states and regions in rebellion. The enslaved people of the loyal border states were deliberately excluded, since Lincoln could not afford to lose Kentucky and Missouri, and the Thirteenth Amendment finished the job in 1865.

s: In the autumn of 1621, the Plymouth colonists held a harvest feast with the Wampanoag.
Massasoit arrived with some ninety men, who brought five deer with them.
Wild fowl was served, along with corn, squash, and shellfish.
Pumpkin pie and cranberry sauce rounded out the meal, just as they do today.
The party lasted three days, with shooting games, military drills, and feasting.
The colonists did not call it a thanksgiving; for them that was a solemn day of prayer.
It became a national holiday only in 1863, when Lincoln set the date in November.
w: No pie and no cranberry sauce. Plymouth had no ovens, no butter, no flour for a crust, and the sugar sat back in England. The menu was venison, wild fowl, corn, squash, and shellfish, and the national holiday had to wait for Lincoln.

s: During the plague years of 1665 and 1666, young Isaac Newton left Cambridge for the family garden at Woolsthorpe.
There, in eighteen months of thinking, he laid the foundations of calculus, optics, and gravitation.
An apple fell from the tree and struck him on the head.
Watching an apple fall set him asking why it must drop straight down toward the earth’s center.
From that question he stretched gravity from the orchard to the Moon and out to the planets.
Newton himself told the story late in life to William Stukeley, who wrote it down in 1726.
Descendants of the tree still grow at Woolsthorpe, raised from cuttings and given to universities.
w: Newton never said the apple hit him on the head. In Stukeley’s memoir he describes watching an apple fall and wondering why it always drops straight down. The knock on the head was added later, to make genius look comic.

s: On the night of April 18, 1775, Paul Revere crossed to Charlestown to warn the countryside that British troops were marching.
His orders were to alert Samuel Adams and John Hancock in Lexington, whom the troops meant to arrest.
Along the road he shouted "The British are coming!" at every farmhouse he passed.
William Dawes rode out of Boston by a second route that same night.
Samuel Prescott was the only rider to carry the alarm all the way to Concord.
A British patrol stopped Revere himself short of Concord and took his horse.
The lone midnight rider of legend came from Longfellow’s poem of 1861, written 86 years after the fact.
w: Revere’s own deposition says the alarm was that the Regulars were coming out; the colonists still considered themselves British, so the famous cry would have made no sense. He never finished the ride either: Dawes rode too, Prescott reached Concord, and Longfellow turned it into a solo run in 1861.

s: Just after five in the morning on April 18, 1906, an earthquake shook San Francisco for under a minute.
The initial shock brought down hundreds of buildings and ruptured water mains across the city.
The earthquake itself flattened the great majority of San Francisco.
It was the fires, burning for three days, that destroyed most of what was lost.
With hydrants dry, crews tried dynamiting firebreaks, which often spread the flames instead.
Enrico Caruso, in town to sing, fled in his nightshirt and vowed never to return.
The city rebuilt fast, and threw a world’s fair nine years later to prove it.
w: The shaking did real damage, but fire took the city: more than four hundred blocks burned over three days while broken mains left the hydrants dry. Insurance clerks marked claims as fire rather than earthquake to dodge the quake clause, which is how historians caught the truth. Caruso kept his vow.

s: Thomas Edison patented his incandescent lamp in 1879, and the world moved indoors after dark.
Humphry Davy had demonstrated electric arc lamps more than seventy years earlier, in 1806.
Joseph Swan lit homes in England with carbon-filament lamps around the same time as Edison.
Edison conjured the whole idea out of nothing, in one stroke of solitary genius.
His real achievement was a durable filament and a complete system: dynamos, wiring, and metering.
In Britain, Swan and Edison ended their patent fight by merging into a single company, Ediswan.
The Menlo Park laboratory tested thousands of filament materials before bamboo settled the question.
w: Edison’s triumph was engineering and business, not lone invention. Davy showed electric light in 1806, Swan matched him almost lamp for lamp, and Edison’s own notebooks admit how much was trial and error. The idea was in the air; Edison made it pay.

s: Karl Benz received the patent for a gasoline-powered automobile in January 1886, a three-wheeler he drove around Mannheim.
Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach had just fitted their light, fast engine to a stagecoach that same year.
Earlier inventors had been building steam road carriages since the 1770s, with mixed success.
In America, the Duryea brothers drove the first gasoline car in 1893, three years before Henry Ford built his first.
Henry Ford invented the automobile himself, single-handed and from scratch.
Ford’s actual breakthrough came in 1913, the moving assembly line, which collapsed the price of a car.
By 1918, roughly half of all the cars in America were Model Ts.
w: Benz patented it in Germany in 1886, and Daimler, Maybach, and the Duryeas all contributed before Ford turned his first wheel. Ford’s genius was mass production: the assembly line made the automobile ordinary.

s: On the night of October 8, 1871, fire broke out in southwest Chicago and raced through a city built of wood.
It burned for two days, destroying some 17,500 buildings and leaving about 100,000 people homeless.
Help poured in from across the country, and Chicago rebuilt into the skyscraper city within a generation.
It all began when Mrs. O’Leary’s cow kicked over a lantern in her barn on De Koven Street.
The cow story came from a newspaper report, and the reporter, Michael Ahern, later admitted he had invented the detail.
The invented culprit was convenient in a city where Irish immigrants were easy to blame.
In 1997 the Chicago City Council formally exonerated Catherine O’Leary and her cow of any wrongdoing.
w: No witness ever placed the cow near the lantern. Ahern’s confession, in 1893, came too late to stop the legend, and the O’Learys bore decades of ridicule for a barn fire whose true cause was never established.

s: Between the 1840s and the 1860s, several hundred thousand emigrants walked the trails west toward Oregon, California, and Utah.
The journey of roughly 2,000 miles took four to six months, and most travelers walked it alongside their wagons to spare the oxen.
The great killer on the trail was the ambush.
In truth, cholera and other diseases killed far more emigrants than violence of any kind.
Accidents did their share too: drownings at river crossings, wagon mishaps, and stray gunshots.
Trading and guiding along the route were everyday business, and diarists recorded attacks as rare and remarkable events.
Graves dotted the trail, but most were dug for fever, not arrows.
w: Epidemic cholera, especially in the 1850s, was the trail’s grim reaper; historians estimate roughly one emigrant in ten died along the way, overwhelmingly of disease. The war-party image came from dime novels far more than from diaries.

s: In the summer of 480 BCE, a Greek force held the narrow pass at Thermopylae against the army of Xerxes.
King Leonidas of Sparta commanded the defense, posted where the mountains and the sea squeezed the road thin.
The numbers were never three hundred: several thousand Greeks from many cities stood in the pass at the start.
When a local named Ephialtes betrayed the mountain path, Leonidas dismissed most of the army and kept a rearguard.
Through it all, Leonidas and 300 Spartans alone held the line to the last man.
They died alongside about 700 Thespians and other allies who stayed to the end as well.
The Greek fleet fought in step at Artemisium offshore, and the epitaph honored the Spartans in words a stranger composed.
w: The famous three hundred were Sparta’s full-citizen core, but ‘alone’ betrays the dead of Thespiae most of all, and the pass held several thousand at first. Herodotus, the main source, is careful about who stood; the films are not.

s: Lady Godiva, wife of Leofric, Earl of Mercia, was a real noblewoman of pre-Conquest England.
She rode naked through the streets of Coventry to shame her husband into lightening the people’s taxes.
The first written account appears in the chronicle of Roger of Wendover, more than 150 years after her death.
Godiva and Leofric are well documented as founders and benefactors of monasteries in the Midlands.
No contemporary record mentions a ride of any kind through Coventry.
The ‘Peeping Tom’ character was bolted on centuries later, appearing in print in the 1600s.
By then the town had a festival, a name, and a story far too good to check.
w: Historians treat the ride as legend: a real eleventh-century countess remembered for religious endowments, wrapped two centuries later in a folk tale about taxes, a peeper, and a horse.

s: In late October 1929, the New York Stock Exchange collapsed across a week of panic selling.
Black Thursday and Black Tuesday saw record trades and record losses, and the market kept sliding for years.
Ruined brokers leapt to their deaths from Wall Street windows all through that autumn.
No such epidemic appears in the city’s mortality statistics for the crash months.
A joke made the rounds anyway, that you had to stand in line to get a window, usually credited to Will Rogers.
The suicide rate in New York barely moved in the weeks after the crash.
The real damage was slower and quieter: bank failures, job losses, and a depression that would last a decade.
w: Economists hunting for the wave of jumps, John Kenneth Galbraith among them, found none; the story sold papers then and has sold movies ever since. The crash’s true toll took years, not a sidewalk.

s: The Colosseum opened in Rome around 80 CE with a hundred days of inaugural games.
Professional gladiators were expensive, trained investments owned by schools and managers.
Two gladiators entered the arena, and only one could ever leave it alive.
Most documented fights ended without a death: the loser could be spared, the missio, at the signal of the game’s sponsor.
Referees, the summa rudis, enforced the rules, and a bout could be stopped or even declared a draw.
Novices died more often than established stars, whose owners priced a death into any contract.
Some gladiators were free volunteers, drawn by prize money, fame, and the roar of the crowd.
w: Epitaphs and arena records show careers of many fights and honorable retirements. Death was always possible and sometimes the point, but the economics of the gladiator school favored the survivor; the guaranteed duel to the death is the movies’ invention.

s: If there was a Trojan War, it belongs to the late Bronze Age, when Mycenaean kings warred against a great city in Asia Minor.
In the tradition, after ten fruitless years of siege the Greeks left a hollow wooden horse on the shore and sailed out of sight.
Hidden inside were picked warriors, waiting for the Trojans to drag the prize through their own gates.
Laocoön warned his countrymen to burn it, and sea serpents crushed him before anyone listened.
Homer tells the whole scheme in the Iliad, his poem of the war’s final year.
The Odyssey remembers the horse as a story told at feasts, years after Troy fell.
The fullest lost telling belonged to the Epic Cycle, poems Homer’s own audience knew.
Excavations at Hisarlik in modern Turkey have uncovered a burned city behind great walls.
w: The Iliad never mentions the horse: it ends with Hector’s funeral, and the trick enters literature through the Odyssey, the lost Epic Cycle, and Virgil’s Aeneid. The horse is real mythology, just not Homer’s.

s: In 1776, David Bushnell of Connecticut built the Turtle, a one-man, hand-cranked wooden submarine.
Its mission was to fix a powder charge beneath a British warship and slip away before the blast.
On a September night in New York Harbor, Sergeant Ezra Lee cranked out against HMS Eagle, the flagship of the fleet.
He worked beneath the hull in darkness and current, and could not drive the auger home.
Nearly out of air, he gave up, and the drifting charge exploded harmlessly in open water.
A second sortie that October sank the Eagle outright, the first warship ever destroyed by a submarine.
The Turtle’s true legacy was proof that a man could move and fight beneath the surface.
w: The Turtle never sank anything; both of its sorties failed, and the Eagle survived the war. The first warship ever sent down by a submarine was the USS Housatonic, destroyed by the hand-cranked Confederate Hunley in Charleston Harbor in 1864.

s: The Pony Express carried letters between St. Joseph, Missouri, and Sacramento, California, beginning in April 1860.
Riders swapped horses at relay stations spaced roughly every ten miles and pushed on day and night.
For twenty years it was the backbone of American cross-country mail.
At its best it moved a letter nearly 3,000 kilometers in ten days, and once raced Lincoln’s inaugural address to California in about a week.
The service lost money from the start, charging dollars for ounces that cost far more to carry.
When the transcontinental telegraph linked the coasts in October 1861, the venture closed after eighteen months.
Its fame owes less to its ledgers than to Buffalo Bill, whose Wild West show put its riders, real and invented, at center stage.
w: Eighteen months, April 1860 to October 1861: the telegraph, not the frontier itself, ended it. The legend was manufactured afterward, by dime novels and by Buffalo Bill Cody’s spectaculars, and it has outlived the telegraph too.

s: The influenza of 1918 killed tens of millions worldwide, more than the war that was still raging.
The pandemic began in Spain, which is why the world named the sickness after that country.
Spain was neutral, and its newspapers were free to report the epidemic while combatant nations censored theirs.
Wartime censorship, not geography, pinned the name on Madrid.
The deadliest wave swept army camps and battle lines in the autumn of 1918.
One of the first documented American outbreaks came at Camp Funston, Kansas, in March 1918.
From there it rode troop ships and railways until hardly a country on Earth was untouched.
w: The name is an artifact of censorship: neutral Spain printed what the combatants suppressed. The strongest early records of the deadly form point to an army camp in Kansas in March 1918, and historians have since traced earlier sparks elsewhere, none of them Spanish.

s: On the night of March 5, 1770, British soldiers fired into a Boston crowd and killed five colonists.
The crowd had spent hours pelting the sentries with snowballs, ice, and firewood, daring them to fire.
Crispus Attucks, a sailor of African and Native descent, was among the dead.
Paul Revere published an engraving of the scene that stoked outrage through the colonies.
The engraving showed the brawl honestly: scattered snow, a surging crowd, and panicked soldiers firing at random.
John Adams defended the soldiers in court and won acquittals for all but two, who were branded for manslaughter.
Patriots called the night a massacre for the sound of the word, and the label has stuck for centuries.
w: Revere’s engraving was propaganda on copper: an ordered volley beneath a customhouse renamed ‘Butcher’s Hall’, no snow anywhere, and a composition borrowed from Henry Pelham without credit. The courtroom, at least, told the messier truth.

t: The Charge of the Light Brigade · 1854
s: On October 25, 1854, at Balaklava in the Crimea, some 670 British light cavalry rode into a valley of Russian guns.
A vague order had sent them after the wrong battery, the one at the valley’s end rather than the captured heights.
Cannon raked them from three sides along the whole length of the ride.
The brigade was annihilated to a man, and not one rider fought his way back.
The French general watching the madness called it splendid, but not war.
Tennyson’s poem, written within weeks, carried the ride into legend.
In truth the riders reached the guns at the valley’s end, overran them, and cut their way out again.
Roughly a third fell, about 110 dead and 160 wounded, and the survivors came home to tell it.
w: Of roughly 670 riders about 110 died; the rest rode back out through the same fire, having briefly overrun the guns at the far end. Tennyson’s ‘noble six hundred’ is elegy, not a body count; the annihilation is a later embellishment.

s: In 1513, Juan Ponce de León sailed north from Puerto Rico and charted a flowery coast he named Florida.
He claimed it for Spain, clashed with the local peoples, and returned twice more.
His royal patent named the Fountain of Youth as the expedition’s purpose.
No document from his lifetime connects him to any such search.
The fountain legend was pinned on him by chroniclers writing after his death, one of them mocking the old man as a fool.
What the crown wanted was land, settlement, and a governor’s title.
He died in 1521 of a wound taken in a skirmish in Florida, still chasing the same prizes.
w: The Fountain of Youth is a posthumous legend: it first appears in a chronicle written years after Ponce died, as a joke at the expense of a vain old man. His expedition records and royal grants mention land and title, never a fountain.

s: On May 10, 1869, the rails of the first transcontinental railroad met at Promontory, in the Utah Territory.
The Central Pacific had clawed east over the Sierra Nevada; the Union Pacific had laid its way west across the plains.
Ceremonial spikes of gold, silver, and Arizona silver were offered up for the last tie.
The final blows were tapped down the telegraph wire to both coasts, and the country celebrated at once.
The famous photographs show the two engines nose to nose, buffered by crowds, champagne, and speeches.
The Central Pacific’s Chinese crews had cut the summit tunnels through two savage Sierra winters.
The junction was made at Promontory Point, a spit of land reaching into the Great Salt Lake.
The site is now a national historical park, and its signs gently correct a very old mistake.
w: It happened at Promontory Summit, not Promontory Point: the Point is a peninsula in the Great Salt Lake some eighty kilometers to the south, while the Summit is a pass on the rail line’s climb. Reporters of the day mostly got it right; the error is a later habit.

s: In 1271, a Venetian teenager set out east with his father and uncle for the court of Kublai Khan.
Marco Polo spent some seventeen years in the Khan’s service, governing a city and inspecting provinces.
Captured at sea in a later war, he dictated his travels to a cellmate in a Genoese prison.
His book introduced Europe to paper money, coal, and a postal service that ran day and night.
Historians still argue over how much he saw himself and how much he retold secondhand.
One of the things he is most famous for bringing home, so the legend goes, is the noodle.
Pasta of every kind was unknown in Italy before his ships docked in Venice in 1295.
w: Italians were eating pasta centuries before Marco Polo was born; Arab rule brought dried noodles to Sicily by the twelfth century. The pasta story was invented by an American trade journal in the 1920s and has been hard to kill ever since.

s: In 1588, Philip II sent about 130 ships up the Channel to escort an invasion army from Flanders.
The English fleet hovered and harried the Armada for a week without winning a clear battle.
Fireships at Calais broke the Armada’s crescent formation, and the squadrons clashed at Gravelines.
Damage and ammunition shortages, not sunk ships, decided the day; both fleets ran low on powder.
The Armada was ordered home the long way, around Scotland and Ireland.
In the Channel fighting, the English sank most of the Spanish ships then and there.
Autumn storms wrecked perhaps half of the fleet on the northern and Irish coasts.
Spain rebuilt its navy and remained a first-rate power at sea for another fifty years.
w: The running fight cost the Spanish only a handful of ships, and Gravelines sank none outright; the real destruction came from storms on the long retreat. The decisive naval victory of legend was mostly weather.

s: On July 14, 1789, a Parisian crowd stormed the Bastille, the royal fortress and state prison.
The garrison, about eighty invalides and thirty-two Swiss, surrendered after hours of fighting.
The crowd had come first for the gunpowder and muskets stored inside.
Nearly a hundred attackers died in the fight, and the governor’s head went on a pike.
Louis XVI woke to the news late; the duc de La Rochefoucauld-Liancourt told him it was not a revolt but a revolution.
Its dungeons held hundreds of prisoners rotting in chains, which is why the crowd came for them.
On the day it fell, the fortress held seven prisoners: four forgers, two madmen, and a wayward aristocrat.
The building was demolished within months, and its stones were carted off for bridges.
w: The Bastille of popular imagination had been emptied long before the Revolution; by 1789 it held a handful of ordinary inmates, and the mob came for powder, not prisoners. The storming was about arms and the symbolism of royal power.

s: The best-loved story of George Washington’s boyhood has him leveling his father’s cherry tree.
Confronted, the six-year-old is supposed to have said that he could not tell a lie.
The tale ran through American schoolbooks for a century and a half.
It first appears in the 1806 edition of Mason Locke Weems’s Life of Washington.
Weems was an itinerant parson turned bookseller with a sure instinct for what would sell.
The first edition of his biography, from 1800, somehow managed to leave the story out.
He had the anecdote from an aged lady who spent her childhood near the Washingtons and remembered it well.
Mount Vernon’s own historians note that the story is, at best, a very old piece of marketing.
w: No contemporary source records the tree; the story surfaces six years after Washington’s death, in a biography that grew taller with every edition. Weems never named a witness, and the aged lady appears nowhere outside his prefaces.

s: In the winter of 1636-37, the Dutch bid astonishing prices for tulip bulbs.
At the peak, contracts for a single rare bulb were said to fetch the price of a canal house.
In February 1637, buyers at a Haarlem auction simply refused to pay, and the market collapsed.
Most of the wildest trades were paper futures; bulbs rarely changed hands at the top prices.
Pamphleteers mocked the mania, and moralists made it a lesson about greed for centuries.
The fallout went to courts and guild committees, which mostly settled debts for pennies.
The crash ruined the whole Dutch economy, and the Golden Age never recovered.
Amsterdam’s trade, banking, and art market carried on as if little had happened.
w: The damage was narrow: a limited circle of speculators and growers took losses while the wider economy barely noticed. The national ruin of legend was largely invented by a Victorian popular history two hundred years later, and it stuck.

s: In late 1932, Australia sent soldiers with machine guns against emus rampaging through Western Australian wheat country.
Perhaps twenty thousand birds were flattening crops and tearing fences in the Campion district.
The gunners found the emus scattered in small, wary mobs that moved like cavalry.
Ambushes at waterholes failed; the birds outran trucks and dodged the first bursts.
After a month and thousands of rounds, the unit was recalled with little to show.
The commanding major praised the birds’ maneuvering, comparing their tactics to Zulus in a dry report.
The campaign ended in a clean victory, the flocks broken and driven from the district.
Fence-building and later bounty culls achieved what the Lewis guns never did.
w: It was a famous failure: fewer than a thousand birds were confirmed killed, the emus kept coming through the wire, and the press ran it as a defeat. The major’s admiration for the emus’ tactics became part of the joke.

t: The Library of Alexandria · c. 48 BCE
s: The library of Alexandria, founded by the Ptolemies, aimed at nothing less than every book in the world.
Ships in the harbor were searched, and visiting texts were seized, copied, and returned.
Eratosthenes used its scholars to measure the Earth; Euclid wrote his Elements in its orbit.
In 48 BCE, Julius Caesar’s fire burned the docks and the warehouses where scrolls were stored.
The institution declined slowly for centuries after, through budget cuts, politics, and neglect.
Whatever survived into the 390s was a shadow of the great collection of the Ptolemies.
The fire took the whole library in a single night, hundreds of thousands of scrolls at once.
The story that Arab conquerors burned it in 640 was debunked long ago by the sources themselves.
w: The fire of 48 BCE destroyed a storehouse of scrolls, not the library; the institution and its descendants limped on for centuries. The overnight annihilation of legend is the myth; the truth is a long, dull fade of funding and neglect.

s: The iron maiden, a spiked cabinet said to close slowly on its victim, headlines every tour of the Middle Ages.
The most famous example, the Virgin of Nuremberg, was a star of German collections for centuries.
Tales credit it with victims beyond counting under medieval princes and inquisitors.
Its first appearances in print come in the 1790s, in German descriptions of an older execution.
The Nuremberg piece itself was assembled in the early 1800s from older parts, as a curiosity.
Medieval court records teem with the machine, named and priced alongside racks and wheels.
No medieval trial, inventory, or account mentions anything of the kind.
Paying audiences and patriotic legend, not torturers, kept it famous.
w: The iron maiden is a fabrication of the 18th and 19th centuries, built for show and for stories about a darker past than the sources support. Not one medieval record names the device; the spikes never closed on a medieval prisoner.

s: Eli Whitney’s cotton gin cleaned short-staple cotton far faster than hand picking, and the South never looked the same.
The gin cleaned the seeds from short-staple cotton, a variety that had been too slow to process to pay.
He patented it in 1794, and the machine spread across the cotton belt within a decade.
The effect was economic dynamite: cotton became king, and the price of enslaved labor rose with it.
His gin was pirated widely, and his patent fights in Georgia courts brought him little profit.
The gin’s fame won Whitney a federal musket contract built on interchangeable parts.
The gin quietly hastened abolition in the South, making hand labor unnecessary and starving the slave system of demand.
Within thirty years the cotton states’ enslaved population had roughly tripled, and abolition had moved further away, not closer.
w: The gin made slavery expand, not fade: by making short-staple cotton profitable it pushed the plantation economy across the Deep South, and the enslaved population of the cotton states roughly tripled in the thirty years after 1790. Whitney’s machine was a force multiplier for the system it was supposed to ease.

s: Gold found on Bonanza Creek in 1896 reached Seattle and San Francisco in July 1897 aboard the Portland, and the stampede began.
Roughly one hundred thousand people set out for the Klondike; fewer than forty thousand ever arrived.
Canadian law required each stampeder to haul a ton of supplies over the passes to prevent starvation.
The most famous image of the rush is the unbroken line of climbers on the Chilkoot in 1898.
The rush built Skagway and Dawson almost overnight, wooden cities of saloons and warehouses.
The gold was easy money: a claim could be worked in a season with nothing but a pan and a shovel.
Most claims were already staked by the time the great mass of stampeders arrived in 1898.
Of those who reached the fields, only a few hundred emerged with any fortune at all, and many lost it within a few years.
w: The creeks were locked in permafrost and the good claims were staked before the stampede arrived; miners burned and boiled their way to bedrock through the winters. The surest profits went to outfitters, saloons, and the boatmen of the Yukon, which is why the rush’s fortunes so often came off the stampeders rather than out of the ground.

t: The War of the Worlds Broadcast · 1938
s: On October 30, 1938, CBS broadcast an adaptation of H.G. Wells’s novel, produced by a young Orson Welles.
The play ran as simulated news bulletins, interrupting a weather report and a dance band.
Newspapers the next morning ran stories of panicked listeners fleeing their homes.
Telephone lines and newspaper desks lit up within minutes of the broadcast.
The panic was a national stampede: crowds fled the roads, and thousands were treated for shock.
Later studies found most listeners knew the program was a play or never heard it at all.
The panic story sold papers and gave radio’s critics a weapon against the networks.
Welles faced the press the next day, and the broadcast made him a celebrity rather than a scapegoat.
w: The mass panic was mostly a newspaper story: researchers find scattered fright, not stampedes, and most of the country never heard the show at all. The papers were fighting radio for advertising, and their coverage of the night became a legend that outran the event; the streets stayed quiet.

s: In 1789 France went bankrupt aiding the American revolution, and the Estates-General met for the first time in 175 years.
The Bastille held seven prisoners the day it fell, and its fall made July 14 the national day.
The Revolution abolished feudal privileges on a single August night in 1789.
The tricolor and the Marseillaise both came out of the revolutionary decade.
The guillotine claimed hundreds of thousands of heads during the Terror alone.
About seventeen thousand official death sentences were handed down during the Terror, most in the provinces.
More lives were lost in the Vendée and the revolutionary wars than under the blade itself.
The guillotine remained France’s official method of execution until the death penalty was abolished in 1981.
w: The blade’s toll was grim but far smaller than the legend: about 16,600 official death sentences during the Terror, only a few thousand of them in Paris. The real killing fields were the Vendée and the revolutionary wars, which took far more lives than the guillotine and never became the symbol.

s: Founded in 1478 under Ferdinand and Isabella, the Spanish Inquisition outlived every institution it policed.
Its tribunals kept meticulous records, which is how historians can count its cases.
It focused on converted Jews and Muslims suspected of secretly practicing their old faiths.
Its autos-da-fé were public ceremonies of penance and punishment, attended by crowds.
The Spanish Inquisition burned hundreds of thousands of heretics at the stake.
It was abolished only in 1834, more than three and a half centuries after it began.
Modern tallies from its own records put executions at a few thousand in all that time.
The Black Legend painted its numbers far larger, to serve the Protestant rivals of Spain.
w: The Inquisition was real and cruel, but its scale was a fraction of the legend: modern tallies from its own records count roughly three to five thousand executions across three and a half centuries. The far larger figures come from Protestant propaganda of the sixteenth century, not from the archive.

s: The mission fell on March 6, 1836, on the thirteenth day of the siege.
Santa Anna’s army entered before dawn, and the fighting inside lasted perhaps ninety minutes.
The garrison’s famous line in the sand, drawn by Travis, first appears in print decades after the battle.
Crockett arrived in February as part of the garrison and died on the final morning.
Every defender died fighting to the last man, rifles in hand; none was taken alive.
A Mexican officer’s diary describes a handful of prisoners put to death on Santa Anna’s order.
The noncombatants inside, women, children, and enslaved workers, survived the battle.
The Alamo’s legend won Texas the reinforcements that settled the revolution at San Jacinto weeks later.
w: The fight to the last man owes more to the stage and the screen than to the battlefield: accounts from the Mexican side describe several defenders captured and put to death on the morning of March 6. Travis’s line in the sand is likewise a story printed decades later; the sources nearest the morning say no such thing.

s: On June 25, 1876, George Custer split his regiment into three battalions near the Little Bighorn.
The Lakota and Northern Cheyenne fielded the largest Native force of the Plains wars.
Custer’s two hundred or so men were wiped out on the ridge within about an hour.
The battle’s survivors were the men under Reno and Benteen, besieged on the bluffs for two days.
Sitting Bull himself led the charge that destroyed Custer’s battalion.
Crazy Horse and Gall led the fighters while Sitting Bull, in his mid-forties, directed from the camp.
Custer’s Crow scouts warned him the village was too big to fight, and he rode on anyway.
News of the defeat reached the East during the centennial summer of 1876, a national shock.
w: Sitting Bull was the moral center of the resistance, not its battlefield commander: in his mid-forties and recovering from the sun dance, he led in counsel while men like Crazy Horse and Gall led in the field. Custer’s battalion died on the ridges; the legend handed the older chief a sword he never carried that day.

s: The Donner party left Missouri in May 1846, a wagon train of about ninety people.
A shortcut advertised in a guidebook, the Hastings Cutoff, cost them weeks in the salt desert.
Snow trapped them at Truckee Lake in early November, a month early.
Relief parties from California reached the camps in February 1847.
Survivors testified to cannibalism in the camps through that winter.
Every survivor of that winter lived by eating the dead.
Not everyone resorted to it; some families refused, and lived on boiled hides and bones.
Of the eighty-one trapped, a little more than half lived, and the disaster made the cutoff’s author infamous.
w: Roughly half the party survived, and not all of them lived on the dead: some survivors, including entire families, refused cannibalism and ate boiled hide, glue, and bones. The resort to it was late and desperate, in a winter the guidebook’s shortcut had made fatal.

s: In June 1633, Galileo Galilei stood trial in Rome before the Inquisition.
He was accused of holding and teaching that the Sun stands still and the Earth moves.
Found vehemently suspect of heresy, he was forced to abjure his opinions and recant.
He was then tortured on the rack until his health broke,
and spent his last nine years confined to a dungeon cell.
Legend has him muttering, after his recantation, that the Earth still moves.
w: Galileo was never tortured and never saw a dungeon. Aged sixty-nine and ill, he was threatened with torture under the formal rules of the day but never touched, and the sentence was house arrest: first in the Medici villa, then his own home near Florence, where he kept working and went blind.

s: In December 1888, in Arles, Vincent van Gogh cut his own ear with a razor.
The night before, he had quarreled bitterly with Paul Gauguin at the Yellow House.
He is said to have wrapped the severed piece and left it at a neighboring house.
The town petitioned to have him confined, and he entered the hospital at Arles within days.
He had cut off the entire ear, and the loss disfigured him for the rest of his life,
though he painted himself with a bandage a month later, and died in 1890, thirty-seven years old.
w: It was part of the ear, not the whole thing. A sketch by the doctor who treated him shows the rim largely gone but the lobe intact, and the whole-ear version grew with the retelling, as the story of the package passed from mouth to mouth.

s: Walt Disney, the animator who built an empire out of a mouse, died of lung cancer in December 1966, ten days after his sixty-fifth birthday.
His body was frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored in a cryonic chamber beneath Disneyland,
where it waits, the story goes, for medicine to catch up with his ambitions.
The tale spread within a few years of his death and has never fully gone away.
The family kept the arrangements strictly private, which fed the rumor for decades.
Disney himself loved futurism, which did not help his case.
w: Disney was cremated, and his ashes lie in Forest Lawn cemetery in Glendale. The cryonics rumor first surfaced in print years after his death and has been debunked ever since by the public record. There is no Disney deep freeze, in Anaheim or anywhere else.

s: In November 1620, the Mayflower settlers landed on the western shore of Cape Cod Bay and founded Plymouth Colony.
The Pilgrims, as they came to be called, had aimed for Virginia but were blown north.
They stepped ashore, the story goes, onto a single boulder now known as Plymouth Rock.
The rock was pointed out by one of the Pilgrims themselves, who marked the spot of the landing,
and the landmark has been guarded and venerated ever since.
Today it rests behind a portico on the Plymouth waterfront.
w: No contemporary source mentions any rock. The boulder enters the record in 1741, when a ninety-four-year-old church elder named Thomas Faunce said his father had pointed it out to him, more than a century after the landing. The Pilgrims never wrote a word about it, and the rock is remembered because the story arrived before the doubters did.

s: The German autobahn is one of the world’s most famous road systems, with long stretches without a speed limit.
Its origin story is tied to the Nazis, who came to power in January 1933.
Construction of the first autobahn began under Hitler’s government that spring, as a make-work project for the unemployed,
and the early motorways became a showcase of the regime’s modernity.
The routes, with their gentle curves and forested medians, still shape German driving today.
Their design standards were much copied abroad.
w: The first motorway generally counted as an autobahn opened in August 1932, under the Weimar Republic: Cologne to Bonn, begun while Hitler was still campaigning in the streets, and opened by the mayor of Cologne, Konrad Adenauer. Hitler’s government expanded and propagandized the network, but it inherited the idea, the first route and even the plans.

s: The Great Sphinx of Giza is a limestone colossus with the body of a lion and the face of a pharaoh, old beyond easy reckoning.
Its missing nose is famously the work of Napoleon’s soldiers, who shot it off for target practice during the Egyptian campaign of 1798,
or so generations of tour guides have repeated.
French sketches from the campaign show the nose already gone, and no diary of the expedition claims the deed.
The face has also lost its ceremonial beard, fragments of which sit in museums today.
The sphinx spent much of its long life buried to the shoulders in sand.
w: The nose was gone long before Napoleon was born. A Danish expedition sketched the face in 1737, already noseless, and an Arab chronicler of the fifteenth century describes the mutilation of the face by a zealot named Muhammad Sa’im al-Dahr, put to death for the deed in 1380. Napoleon’s men came too late to be the culprits, and they brought scholars who drew exactly what they saw.

s: In May or June 1776, according to the family story, a secret committee from Congress visited a Philadelphia upholsterer.
The visitors included George Washington, and they carried a sketch of a new flag for a new nation.
The seamstress, a widow named Betsy Ross, suggested a five-pointed star in place of the sketch’s six-pointed one, folding a square of cloth so a single snip would cut it.
Congress then adopted her flag as the first official banner of the United States,
and her house on Arch Street is now a shrine visited by hundreds of thousands.
The circle-of-stars flag remains the best-loved design of the early republic.
w: There is no record of any of it. Congress did not adopt the stars and stripes until June 1777, a year after the supposed visit, and the whole story rests on a paper read by her grandson to a historical society in 1870, nearly a century after the fact. Even the circle of stars cannot be pinned to her: its first surviving depictions are from the nineteenth century.

s: Canute, king of England, Denmark and Norway, was among the most powerful rulers of the eleventh century.
His court, by his own account, was full of flatterers who insisted that all things obeyed him.
To teach them a lesson, he had his throne carried to the shore and commanded the incoming tide to halt, and the sea obeyed him,
wetting only the courtiers while the king stayed dry.
The story comes from the chronicle of Henry of Huntingdon, writing a century later.
It entered the folk history of England and never left.
w: In the chronicle, the sea ignores him completely. Canute sits through the rising water until it soaks him and his robes, then declares that the power of kings is empty beside the power that holds the heavens, and hangs his crown on a crucifix at Winchester, never wearing it again. The version with the obedient sea turns the whole moral inside out.

s: The Flavian Amphitheatre, known as the Colosseum, opened in 80 CE with a hundred days of games.
It could hold fifty thousand spectators, seated by law and rank, and stands among the wonders of the ancient world.
The arena floor concealed cages and lifts that sprang beast and man into the light.
There, for three centuries, crowds watched uncounted Christian martyrs thrown to the lions,
a persecution memorialized by popes and pilgrims.
The building has been a place of Christian veneration since the eighteenth century.
w: There is no evidence that any Christian was martyred in the Colosseum. Not one ancient source connects a named martyr to the building; the tradition grew around its ruined grandeur in later centuries, helped along when a pope put a stop to its quarrying in 1749, and historians have called the slaughter of Christians there a legend ever since.

s: The Hundred Years War between England and France began in 1337 with a dynastic quarrel over the French crown.
It lasted precisely one hundred years, ending at the Battle of Castillon in 1437,
and its five generations saw Crecy, Poitiers and Agincourt, Joan of Arc and the Treaty of Troyes.
The war’s length made standing armies, taxation and national feeling permanent fixtures of both kingdoms.
Chaucer and Froissart wrote against its background.
The name itself was invented by later historians, not by anyone who fought in it.
w: It ran a hundred and sixteen years. Castillon, the last battle, was fought in 1453, and no formal peace was ever sealed: the war ended because both sides were spent, with England holding nothing in France but Calais. The tidy name dates from the nineteenth century, and the tidy hundred from nowhere at all.

s: Roman banquets of the wealthy ran for hours through course after course of extravagant food.
To make room for more, the diners would retire to a special room to purge themselves, called the vomitorium,
and then return to the table for the next round.
The practice, whatever its real extent, became shorthand for Roman excess.
Satirists and moralists, Juvenal among them, skewered the appetites of the age.
The word itself is Latin, from a verb for spewing.
w: A vomitorium is an exit. The word belongs to amphitheatres and stadiums: the arched passages that let a crowd pour out quickly, named for the spewing of people, not of diners. The purge-room of legend appears nowhere in Roman writing; it is a modern misunderstanding of a good architectural term, dressed up as scandal.

s: A fully armed knight of 1400 wore plate from head to toe, articulated at every joint.
A complete harness weighed around fifty pounds, most of it carried on the shoulders and spread down the limbs.
So great was the burden that knights had to be lowered onto their horses by cranes,
and once unhorsed they lay helpless, like overturned beetles, until squires hoisted them upright.
The crane rig, sometimes called the three-point landing, appears in books to this day.
Field armor was fitted to its owner like a bespoke suit.
w: Knights were lowered onto horses by cranes only in fiction. Fifty pounds, no more than a modern infantryman’s pack, is spread across the body, and plate is articulated: knights mounted unaided, fought on foot and rose from the ground with ease. Contemporary records describe men in full harness climbing onto horses and turning somersaults; the crane belongs to Mark Twain’s Connecticut Yankee and to Laurence Olivier’s Henry V film, not to the fifteenth century.

s: In June 1963, President Kennedy stood before the wall in West Berlin and delivered one of the Cold War’s most famous speeches.
In the crowd’s ears, his declaration ‘Ich bin ein Berliner’ meant ‘I am a jelly doughnut’,
because a Berliner is a kind of filled pastry as well as a citizen of the city,
and the story of the laughing crowd has been retold ever since.
He had rehearsed the phrase with a translator before the speech.
The address remains the best-remembered American statement of the Cold War.
w: Berliners understood Kennedy exactly. In Berlin the jam pastry is called a Pfannkuchen; the word Berliner for it belongs to other regions, and in any case ‘Ich bin ein Berliner’ is the standard German way to declare solidarity with the city. The doughnut joke surfaces decades after the speech, and no reporter present in 1963 recorded any laughter.

s: The Colossus of Rhodes, a bronze statue of the sun god Helios, was finished around 280 BCE after twelve years of work.
It stood over thirty meters tall, roughly the height of the Statue of Liberty without her pedestal,
and ranked among the wonders of the ancient world.
It famously straddled the harbor mouth, with ships sailing between its legs,
an image printed on old maps and souvenirs ever since.
It stood only fifty-six years before an earthquake broke it at the knees.
w: It never straddled anything. The harbor-spanning colossus is an invention of late-medieval artists; ancient accounts put the statue standing beside, not over, the harbor, and the bronze techniques of the day could not have built a straddling figure in any case. Ships did not sail between its legs until engravers decided they should.

s: Stonehenge, the great ring of standing stones on Salisbury Plain, took shape in stages across more than a thousand years.
Its largest stones, the sarsens, were raised around 2500 BCE, dragged some thirty kilometers to the site.
The ring was built as a temple by the Druids, the ancient priesthood of the British Isles,
and their rites at the stones are remembered every midsummer.
Roman writers described the Druids of Britain, and later antiquaries joined the priesthood to the stones at a stroke.
Modern dating put the circle far older than those first guesses.
w: The Druids came far too late. Stonehenge was already ancient when the Iron Age priesthood existed: the sarsen ring was complete by around 2500 BCE and the site was in ruins and reuse long before the Druids of Roman accounts. The link was suggested by seventeenth-century antiquaries, and modern druids gather at a monument their ancestors never knew.

s: In June 1752, a kite carrying a key rose into the Philadelphia sky,
in the most famous experiment in American science.
Benjamin Franklin had designed it to draw electrical fire from a passing cloud,
and he flew it himself through the storm, his young son at his side.
The letter he wrote to the Royal Society that autumn describes the experiment,
and the danger he ran was clear to everyone who read it.
w: No witness ever described Franklin flying that kite. The famous letter to the Royal Society explains how to perform the experiment, a recipe for others more than a report; his son William was a grown man of twenty-two, not a boy, and the one person we know repeated it properly, Georg Richmann of St Petersburg, was killed by a bolt the next summer. Franklin probably stayed indoors.

s: In 1581, Oda Nobunaga invaded the ninja strongholds of Iga province,
and the shadow warriors of Japan passed into legend.
Real ninja were spies and guerrillas, trained in infiltration and escape.
In their craft they famously dressed all in black,
the better to vanish into the night,
or so the woodblock prints always showed them.
w: Real ninja dressed to be ignored: farmer’s clothes, merchant’s robes, the dress of the crowd they were hiding in. The all-black suit is stage costume, borrowed from the black-robed stagehands of Japanese theatre, and an infiltrator wearing it in the street would have been arrested on sight.

s: The machine that defined the French Revolution first fell in April 1792,
designed and built by Dr. Joseph-Ignace Guillotin, the physician who invented it,
as a punishment quick, clean and identical for every rank.
The Assembly thanked him by giving it his name,
and the device cleared the Place de la Révolution by the cartload.
The good doctor was lucky enough to die in his own bed in 1814.
w: Guillotin neither designed nor built it. He only proposed that decapitation, then a privilege of nobles, be extended to all; the machine was engineered by Antoine Louis with the German harpsichord maker Tobias Schmidt, and Guillotin spent his life trying to lose the name, which his family later begged to have changed.

s: Vincent van Gogh died in July 1890, aged thirty-seven, after a decade of painting.
He left behind some two thousand works, canvases alive with color that nobody wanted.
The Red Vineyard went to a Belgian painter for a few hundred francs,
the single sale of his career,
or so the saddest story in art has always told itself.
Everything else gathered dust with his brother Theo.
w: One oil sold for money is documented, The Red Vineyard in 1890, but the whole-life count is wrong: his dealer uncle Cornelis bought nineteen works in a single 1883 order, he bartered canvases with fellow artists for meals and materials, and what made him famous was not bad luck but his sister-in-law, who spent her life selling the estate he left.

s: The national pastime of the United States was invented in 1839
by Abner Doubleday, a cadet who scratched the first diamond in the dirt at Cooperstown,
or so the commission that looked into it concluded in 1907.
The game grew from that schoolyard into the major leagues,
and the Hall of Fame stands on the spot to this day,
a shrine to a single moment of invention.
w: There is no evidence Doubleday, a career artillery officer, ever saw a baseball game, and he was at West Point in 1839, not Cooperstown. The story traces to one old man’s letter collected by a commission run by the sport’s founding magnate, determined to prove the game American; its true parents are older bat-and-ball games, refined in New York in the 1840s by the Knickerbocker club under Alexander Cartwright.

s: In 490 BCE, the Athenians crushed the first Persian landing at Marathon.
A runner was sent to carry the news to the city, roughly forty kilometers away.
He reached the assembly, shouted the victory,
and fell dead on the spot,
the run preserved in the race that bears the plain’s name.
That is how the story was told in the earliest Greek histories, where it appears again and again.
w: Herodotus, writing within living memory, tells of Pheidippides running to Sparta, about 240 kilometers, and says nothing of any death at Athens; the dying messenger first appears in Lucian, a satirist, six hundred years after the battle. The modern race distance is another legend entirely, borrowed from the 1908 London Olympics.

s: Every few years, the lemmings of the Arctic tundra begin to march.
Driven by instinct and overpopulation, they surge across the countryside in swarms,
and when they meet the sea they hurl themselves in, drowning by the thousand.
Nature documentary cameras have caught the spectacle,
most famously in a Disney film of 1958.
The cycles of their numbers are one of the rhythms of the north.
w: Lemmings do migrate in booms, sometimes swimming rivers and drowning in numbers, but they do not commit suicide. The famous 1958 film staged the scene: the producers bought the animals and herded them into a river in Alberta, turning a camera trick into a natural legend.

s: In the arena, the matador goes to work with his cape.
The bull charges the cloth again and again, drawn on by the movement,
because the animal is engaged by the swirl of the fabric,
and above all by its red color.
The cape is even named for it, la muleta, the little red cloth,
