and the bull never learns to stop charging.
w: Cattle are red-green colorblind; the bull cannot tell the cape from the sand by hue and charges the moving cloth, not its color. The red is theater, chosen to mask the blood, and it is the breeding of fighting bulls for aggression, not their eyes, that supplies the charge.

s: In the 1790s, Lazzaro Spallanzani blinded bats in his laboratory and they still flew,
the first hint that the animal hunts with something other than eyes.
Schoolbooks, however, kept the old saying,
because everyone knows that bats are blind,
and the myth taught children about the world of sound.
The truth of echolocation waited until the late 1930s.
w: Bats are not blind; most see about as well as people in dim light, which is exactly what Spallanzani concluded two centuries ago. His blinded bats flew because sound replaced sight, though he could not prove it; that secret held until microphones, thirty years into the twentieth century, caught the calls the ears of the bat had always heard.

s: Lightning never strikes the same place twice, says the old proverb,
and the survivor of one strike is safe from the next.
Roy Sullivan, a park ranger in the Shenandoah mountains, was struck in 1942,
and that, said the proverb, was the end of his luck.
Yet lightning is famously drawn to a single unlucky man,
and rangers in Virginia will tell you the rest of the story.
w: Lightning plays favorites with places and with people: Sullivan was struck seven documented times between 1942 and 1977, once while inside a ranger station, and the Empire State Building takes about two dozen strikes a year. The proverb is a comforting rhyme with nothing behind it.

s: The Empire State Building opened in 1931, the tallest thing on Earth.
Drop a coin from its observation deck and it falls three hundred meters.
By the street it is traveling fast enough to kill a pedestrian,
a fact every New Yorker has been warned about since the tower went up.
The guards have confiscated millions of innocent pennies,
and the sidewalks below are safe only because of the railings.
w: A penny tumbles as it falls, air resistance caps its speed near fifty kilometers an hour, and it lands with the sting of a thrown pebble, no more. The legend of the killer coin ignores drag, the physics every parachute ever packed; the observation deck guards the railings, not the city below.

s: Fill a sink, pull the plug, and watch the water turn.
In the southern hemisphere it drains clockwise, in the north counterclockwise,
so the hotel guides on the equator demonstrate it twice a day.
The Coriolis force from the turning Earth does steer the ocean basins,
though its power over a small basin is a thousand times weaker than the leftover swirl.
A physicist proved the principle with a still tank, hours of waiting and perfect symmetry.
w: In a real sink the whirl is set by the shape of the basin and the motion left in the water, not the hemisphere; the Coriolis effect is a thousand times too weak over a tub. Under laboratory conditions, a still, symmetric tank drained after hours of rest will show it, which is how Ascher Shapiro at MIT proved the principle in 1962; the equator demonstrations run the same bucket of water both ways.

s: Summer is hot and winter is cold, and the reason is the sky.
Kepler explained the orbit in 1609, an ellipse with the Sun off center.
Because the path is not round, the distance between Earth and Sun changes through the year,
and the seasons swing with that distance.
Summer is the half of the year we are closer in, and winter the half we are farther out.
It is a tidy picture, and almost everyone believes it.
w: The seasons come from the tilt of Earth’s axis, about twenty-three degrees, which tips one hemisphere toward the Sun for half the year; the distance story has a fatal flaw, namely that the northern summer falls at aphelion, the farthest point of the orbit. Australia basks while Earth is most distant; distance runs a weak third behind tilt and daylight hours.

s: Humans use only a tenth of their brains, the old claim goes.
The idea was popular around 1908, when the age of self-improvement dawned.
Nine tenths of the organ sit dark and idle,
waiting for the person who learns to switch them on.
Every genius from history proves the point by using more,
which is why so many courses promise to sell the trick.
w: Brain scans show no silent reserve: even during sleep the whole organ hums, and no injury or surgery has ever revealed ninety percent going spare. The saying seems to descend from a misreading of early neurology and the era’s enthusiasm for unused potential; evolution does not cart a tenth-used organ around at twenty watts for nothing.

s: William Harvey proved in 1628 that blood circulates, running in a loop.
Look at a wrist and the veins show blue through the skin.
That is the color of the blood inside, blue as a river,
because blood turns red only when it touches the air in a wound.
Deoxygenated blood is blue in the body, red in the open,
a fact every school nurse has repeated.
w: Blood is never blue; short of oxygen it is dark red, and it meets the air inside the lungs, not at the wound. Veins look blue because skin scatters red light on its way back out; cut a vein and the blood that wells up is dark red at once. The blue-blooded nobility of the old joke have the same red rivers as everyone.

s: Every parent knows the pattern: cake at the party, wildness for an hour.
In the 1970s the link was given a name, hyperactivity from sugary food.
Dozens of studies since have charted the effect on children,
and all that candy reliably sends them bouncing off the walls.
The Feingold diet of 1973 built a whole therapy on the idea,
and candy still gets blamed at every birthday in the world.
w: The controlled studies find no rush: children given sugar behave the same, and in double-blind trials adults rate the behavior of kids who had none as wilder if told they had some. The effect is the setting, the expectation and the party; the hyperactivity diets of the seventies were aimed at additives and have not fared much better.

s: In 1940, British pilots were fighting the night sky over their island.
John Cunningham, a legendary night ace called Cats Eyes,
was famous for his kill tally after dark,
which he owed, the Ministry told the papers, to a diet heavy in carrots.
The story boosted the vegetable and the public planted gardens of them,
and the carrot’s reputation for night sight survived the war.
w: Carrots carry vitamin A, and a deficiency of it dims the eyes, but a healthy person sees no better after a crate of them. The real secret in 1940 was airborne radar, a hush-hush system the RAF preferred not to advertise, so the carrot story made useful cover; Cunningham’s nickname did the rest, and children have been finishing their vegetables for a myth ever since.

s: A fledgling fluttering in the grass looks abandoned.
Every child is warned the same way: touch it and the mother will know.
Birds, the warning goes, will abandon a nest that smells of human hands,
and the chick will be left to starve in the grass.
Audubon painted the parents returning to the branch regardless,
but the warning still gets repeated every spring.
w: Most songbirds have a weak sense of smell and no instinct against human scent; returned chicks are fed as before, and a mother will tolerate a brief inspection of her eggs. The danger of handling is real but different: stress, and being moved so far the parents cannot find them, not the smell of the hand.

s: In 1913, Theodore Roosevelt traveled the rivers of Brazil.
At one stop, his hosts staged a demonstration of the local fish,
a pool of piranhas herded there for the occasion.
A wounded cow was driven in and stripped to the bone in minutes,
the spectacle the former president described with awe in his book,
and nothing in the rivers, he concluded, was a more murderous fish.
w: Roosevelt wrote it all down, but the locals had netted the school beforehand and penned it without food for weeks, a detail he noted with rueful honesty. Wild piranhas school for safety, not for hunts, and eat mostly fish, fruit and fins; the cow-eating swarm is a staged famine, which is why swimmers in the Amazon come home whole every day.

s: Sharks, the story goes, never get cancer.
A book of 1992 built an industry on the claim,
selling shark cartilage as a cancer treatment to the desperate.
The fish seemed proof that nature kept a shield,
since a creature that old and that armored had beaten the disease entirely.
The demand emptied stretches of ocean of sharks for nothing.
w: Sharks get cancer, including cancers of their cartilage; the first tumor of a shark was recorded in 1908 and later papers logged dozens of cases. The cartilage cure failed every controlled trial, and the fishing fleets it launched stripped the sea of animals that had never promised anything but a good story.

s: Crack your knuckles and the sound tells the story.
Bubbles of gas in the joint fluid burst with the pull,
a sound every grandmother has called the sound of arthritis.
A doctor in California tested it properly on himself,
cracking one hand for sixty years and not the other,
and the results won him an Ig Nobel prize in 2009.
w: The California doctor, Donald Unger, cracked the knuckles of his left hand for more than sixty years and left the right alone, and his hands aged alike; the prize he won, in 2009, was for testing his mother’s warning. Larger studies agree: knuckle cracking does not wear the joints, and the pops are gas bubbles forming, not bones grinding.

s: King Camp Gillette patented his razor in 1904, and the shave changed.
Since then young shavers have been warned to wait,
because each shave makes the hair come back thicker and darker,
a fact that has sent adolescents to the barber for advice.
Stubble feels coarser than the original growth,
and the chin of a daily shaver proves the point.
w: Shaving cuts hair at the skin and leaves a blunt tip that feels stubbly; the follicle beneath, which sets thickness, color and rate, never learns what happened above the surface. Hair regrowing after a shave feels coarser for its square-cut edge and shows darker against the skin, but it is neither thicker nor darker in fact.

s: In December 1945, five Navy bombers vanished off Florida on a training flight,
and the rescue plane sent after them was never seen again.
The stretch of sea between Miami, Bermuda and Puerto Rico had its name by the fifties,
and the count of lost ships and planes grew with every retelling.
Insurance underwriters and the Coast Guard finally took a look,
and confirmed the triangle as the deadliest water on Earth.
w: The insurers found nothing: Lloyd’s of London does not charge extra for the triangle, and the Coast Guard’s records show losses there at rates ordinary for the traffic and weather. The vanishings dissolve into storms, wartime sinkings and the accidents of a very busy sea lane; the 1945 flight, as the Navy concluded, was failed compasses, an instructor convinced he was over the Florida Keys, and five planes flying until the fuel ran out.

s: Suetonius, the gossip columnist of the Caesars, tells the story of Incitatus,
the favorite horse of the emperor Caligula.
The animal lived in a marble stable, fed on oats mixed with gold flakes,
and was, the historian records, formally made a consul of Rome.
Priests were said to attend him, and guests were invited to dine at his manger.
The horse’s career is the emblem of an emperor gone mad.
w: Suetonius wrote that Caligula planned to make Incitatus a consul, and Cassius Dio, decades later, dressed it up as done; no list of Rome’s consuls carries a horse. The marble stable and the retinue of servants are possible, an emperor’s joke at the expense of the senatorial class he despised, and the story grew by retelling, as court gossip does. The horse never held office.

s: Sparta raised its sons on hardship and its numbers by severity.
Infants were examined at birth by the elders of the city,
and any judged weak were left out on the mountainside to die.
The site was the Apothetae, the deposition place above the city,
where generations of castoffs were left at the cliff’s edge.
Excavation of the spot has turned up the bones of the babies.
w: Spartan writers mention exposure in principle, but the dig at the Apothetae cliff found no infant bones: the remains were of adults, mostly young men. Weak babies seem to have been left where they could be taken in, an old Mediterranean custom, and the mountain cliff hurling is a later horror story told about a hard people, not by them.

s: Atlantis first appears in two dialogues of Plato, the Timaeus and the Critias.
There he describes a mighty island beyond the Pillars of Heracles,
a power that ruled the outer sea nine thousand years before his day,
destroyed in a single day and night of misfortune.
Plato meant it as a true chronicle of a drowned kingdom,
and sailors have hunted for it ever since.
w: Plato says the opposite: the tale comes to us, he writes, as a story told at a festival, and the dialogue plainly sets Atlantis beside the ideal city of the Republic as a mirror for Athens. No Greek of his time records the island, no trace has surfaced on any seabed, and the endless identifications, Santorini, Spain, Antarctica, all begin by assuming a philosopher was writing a gazetteer.

s: Howard Carter opened the tomb of Tutankhamun in 1922, its gold intact after three thousand years.
Within weeks Lord Carnarvon, the dig’s patron, was dead in Cairo of an infected mosquito bite.
The papers invented a curse on all who entered,
and the death list grew with every retelling: dozens, the story went, within a decade.
A study decades later counted the people who went into the tomb and lived,
and confirmed the curse as the excavation’s most lethal find.
w: Carnarvon died of blood poisoning from a shaving cut on a mosquito bite, in an era before antibiotics, and the rest of the record dissolves: of the people present at the opening, most lived into their seventies and eighties, and Carter himself died of lymphoma seventeen years later. A study of the dig’s personnel found their lifespans ordinary; the curse was written by novelists and sold by the newspapers of the day, hungry for a haunted tomb.

s: In 1607, Jamestown was a starving fort in a hostile country.
Captain John Smith was captured by Powhatan warriors and brought before the chief.
The story is famous: he was laid out for execution, clubs raised,
when the chief’s daughter, a girl of about ten, threw herself over him and saved his life,
an episode Smith recorded in his own contemporary account of the colony,
and the beginning of the most famous rescue in American history.
w: Smith’s own 1608 account of his captivity describes ceremony, gifts and a welcome, and no execution at all; the dramatic rescue appears only in his 1624 retelling, seventeen years later, too convenient to check. The girl was about ten and Smith twenty-seven; Pocahontas later married the tobacco planter John Rolfe, bore a son, saw England, and died at Gravesend in 1617, aged about twenty-one.

s: Rome’s last western emperor was packed off in 476, and the lamps went out.
For a thousand years after, the story goes, Europe thought and built almost nothing.
No scientist worked, no engine turned, no book of note was written,
until the printing press and the Renaissance finally relit the world.
The centuries between Rome and Gutenberg are a blank,
and historians still call them the Dark Ages for a reason.
w: The blank is imaginary. The so-called dark centuries carry the Carolingian renaissance, the first universities, the mechanical clock, eyeglasses and Gothic engineering, and in Baghdad and Córdoba a golden age of astronomy, medicine and algebra; the phrase Dark Ages was coined by writers praising their own era, and historians have been apologizing for it ever since.

s: Billy the Kid was shot dead in 1881, aged twenty-one.
The famous count of his victims stands at twenty-one,
one for each year of his short, violent life.
The number comes from the outlaw’s own boasts to the newspapers,
polished by the men who printed dime novels about him,
and the graveyard marker still carries it today.
w: The Kid, whose real name was likely Henry McCarty, killed four men by the strictest historical count, and took part in a handful of bloody shootouts besides. The twenty-one-for-twenty-one figure was invented by journalists and dime novelists while he was alive; the famous grave marker at Fort Sumner has been stolen and recarved so many times that it lives behind a cage, still advertising a number he never reached.

s: The tower that opened the 1889 World’s Fair rose from the Champ de Mars in two years.
Gustave Eiffel, the bridge engineer, designed every curve of it himself,
and Paris signed its skyline over to his name.
The structure was meant to stand twenty years and then come down,
and only the usefulness of its antenna saved it from the scrap dealers.
Today it is the most visited paid monument on Earth.
w: The first sketch of the tower was drawn by Maurice Koechlin and Émile Nouguier, two junior engineers in the firm, shaped with the architect Stephen Sauvestre; Eiffel bought the rights, championed the design publicly and let his name take the credit, which he defended with publicity for the rest of his life. The firm’s engineers built it; the entrepreneur wore it.

s: Witchcraft trials swept Europe for three centuries, burning thousands at the stake.
The Inquisition ran many of the pyres, and the Church handed down the sentences.
The great hunts peaked in the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries,
nine million witches went to the fire across Europe by the old count,
and the panic ran from village quarrels to courts of law.
Historians have tallied the trials and the sentences for centuries.
w: The old count is off by two orders of magnitude: modern tallies of trial records put executions across three centuries at roughly forty to sixty thousand, and the hunts were an early-modern phenomenon, peaking between 1560 and 1630, when medieval courts and the Inquisition had largely lost interest. The mass burnings belong to the age of the printing press, not the age of cathedrals.

s: Dom Pérignon, the Benedictine cellar master of Hautvillers, died in 1715 after a life among the barrels.
He is the patron saint of the bubble, the legendary inventor of champagne,
and the quote is in every tasting room in the world:
come quickly, I am drinking the stars.
The monk wrestled the wild second fermentation into the bottle at last,
and the wine of kings was born in a monastic cellar.
w: Pérignon spent his career fighting bubbles, not perfecting them: the refermentation that made the fizz ruined his still wine, and his rules aimed at stillness. The stars quotation was invented long after his death, first appearing in a nineteenth-century advertisement, and the sparkling method was already known in England, where scientists and cider makers had bottled fizz before the monk ever pulled a cork.

s: In 1683, the armies of the Ottoman Empire besieged Vienna.
Bakers working in the cellars below the walls heard the enemy digging,
raised the alarm and saved the city, so the story runs.
They celebrated with a bread shaped like the crescent on the enemy’s banners,
and the croissant was born in that victory,
spreading from Austria to Paris after the war.
w: No document ties the croissant to 1683, and the legend first appears in print in the twentieth century. The pastry that reached Paris was the kipferl, an Austrian crescent roll, brought by an entrepreneur who opened the Boulangerie Viennoise in the 1830s; the puff-paste croissant is a French remake of the nineteenth century. Vienna’s bakers may well have heard Turks digging, but they never got a pastry for it.

s: After the battle of Culloden in 1746, the British banned Highland dress.
The kilt, ancient garment of the clans, was driven underground for a generation.
The ban was lifted in 1782, and the tartan returned with the romance of Walter Scott.
The great belted plaid of the Highlands is genuinely old,
wound over the shoulder and worn by centuries of clansmen.
The pleated skirt as the world knows it is the same old garment, cut a little shorter.
w: The pleated skirt is an eighteenth-century invention, not a shortened plaid: the small kilt or philabeg appears in the 1720s, and one account credits its tailoring to Thomas Rawlinson, an English Quaker ironmaster who wanted a safer garment for his Highland furnace workers. The great plaid was the clansmen’s dress; the little kilt is its modern descendant, younger than the ban that briefly suppressed it.

s: Egyptian embalmers of the New Kingdom were masters of their craft.
They preserved the heart, seat of thought and the soul’s anchor, in its place.
The liver, lungs, stomach and intestines went into four canopic jars under gods’ protection.
The brain, too, was carefully preserved in a fifth vessel beside them.
It was, after all, the organ the Egyptians honored above all but the heart.
The tombs tell us so through the embalmers’ own records.
w: The brain was thrown away. Embalmers broke through the ethmoid bone, drew the organ out through the nose in pieces and discarded it; thinking belonged to the heart, and the brain’s only job, as the Egyptians saw it, was to drain mucus. The four jars hold viscera, never a brain, and no fifth vessel existed; early modern writers began the confusion, and the fifth-jar story stuck.

s: Of the seven wonders of the ancient world, six have left their ruins where we can find them.
The Hanging Gardens of Babylon are the exception:
a palace of terraced gardens watered by machines, built, the Greeks said, for a homesick queen.
Excavation of Babylon has traced the terraces, the wells and the great vaults,
matching the descriptions of the ancient writers.
Only the columns themselves have crumbled beyond recognition.
w: A century of digging at Babylon has found no trace of them, and Nebuchadnezzar’s own inscriptions, which list every boast, never mention a garden. Some scholars now argue the wonder stood at Nineveh, built by Sennacherib a century earlier, described in texts that later writers confused with Babylon; either way, the gardens exist only in Greek descriptions, and the site is the only wonder that keeps its secret.

s: The Silk Road carried silk, spices, paper and plague between China and the Mediterranean.
Merchants traveled its whole length for two thousand years,
crossing deserts and passes from Chang’an to Antioch.
They knew it as the Silk Road, the name they had always used,
and traders at either end spoke of it in one word.
The road died only when the sea routes took its trade.
w: No merchant ever called it that, and no ancient text does: the name was coined in 1877 by Ferdinand von Richthofen, a German geographer, for his maps and lectures. Silk indeed went west and much else went both ways, but the people on it knew only the next town, the next oasis and the next commission; the road as a single named thing is a modern invention the ancients would not recognize.

s: When Cortés landed on the coast of Mexico in 1519, the Aztec world read omens in the sky.
Moctezuma, its emperor, hesitated before the strangers,
who came from the sea the prophecies had named.
The Aztecs took the armored visitor for the returning god Quetzalcoatl himself,
and the conquest succeeded because an empire mistook a man for a god.
Moctezuma’s messengers brought the emperor feathers, not warnings.
w: The god story comes almost entirely from post-conquest accounts written by and for the victors, and the earliest Spanish letters say nothing of it; Moctezuma’s own first messages treated Cortés as a foreign lord, an ambassador to be managed, not a deity. The Quetzalcoatl identification hardened decades later, as the Spanish explained their victory as destiny; an emperor who believed no such thing was made into a dupe by the conquerors’ history.

s: In the weightlessness of orbit, a pen is a problem: ink will not fall to the nib.
NASA spent years and millions of dollars inventing a pressurized space pen,
while the Russian program solved it in one move: the cosmonauts used a pencil.
The Fisher Space Pen reached orbit in the late sixties,
sold to both space programs alike.
It is the parable everyone loves, of the simple solution beating the expensive one.
w: NASA spent no such money: the pen was developed privately by Paul Fisher’s company, which spent its own million dollars, and the space agency bought the result at a fair price; the Soviet program bought the same pens. Pencils, in fact, were the hazard: broken tips and flammable graphite drifting into instrument panels got both programs looking for something safer. The parable was never true, but it refuses to die.

s: Everyone knows the rule: drink eight glasses of water a day.
It descends from dietary guidance of the 1940s, which set about two liters for adults.
Food, coffee, tea and fruit do not count toward the total.
Only pure water keeps the balance, and the eight glasses are a floor, not a ceiling,
so a person who drinks less runs a deficit that quietly taxes the kidneys.
The rule has survived every change in diet fashion since.
w: The 1940s guideline did say about two liters a day, but the same paragraph said most of it comes with your food; the recommendation was never eight glasses on top of meals. Water from coffee, tea, milk and soup counts nearly the same as tap water, and thirst is the guide healthy bodies have used forever; the kidney cares about total fluid, not its packaging. The eight-glass number appears in no clinical guideline anywhere.

s: Legend puts the founding of Rome in 753 BCE.
Twin boys, sons of Mars and a doomed princess, were set adrift on the Tiber in a basket.
A she-wolf found them at the river’s edge and suckled them,
until a herdsman took the pair home and raised them as shepherds.
Romulus killed his brother in a quarrel and founded the city on the Palatine,
and archaeology has since confirmed the wolf, the twins and the year.
w: The wolf story is legend, told to give the city a divine ancestor and a moral about fratricide; Roman historians themselves argued about it, and Livy calls the tale suited to poetry rather than history. Excavation under the Palatine has found Iron Age huts from about the eighth century BCE, real people in a real village, but no wolf, no basket and no twins. The founding date was assigned centuries later, working backward from lists of kings, and the birthday is a guess that became a festival.

s: After the legions left Britain, a war leader held the island against the Saxons.
Battles at a place called Badon gave the Britons a generation of peace.
The man in the middle of it was Artorius, Riothamus, Arthur,
a king in shining mail with a round table of knights and a sword from a lake.
Geoffrey of Monmouth wrote the history down from older records,
and the English have been finding his castle ever since.
w: No contemporary text names Arthur at all: the first mention, in a ninth-century Welsh annal, is two lines, one about Badon and one about a battle where Arthur and Medraut fell, with no sword, table or empire. Geoffrey of Monmouth’s twelfth-century history invented the king the world knows and cited no sources; the round table, Lancelot and the lake came later, in French. A war leader may well have existed; the king of the legend is literature, beginning to end.

s: The greenwood hero is old: a 1377 poem already passes him along.
He robbed the rich to feed the poor, with Maid Marian and the Merry Men in Sherwood.
The ballads give his true identity as Robert Hood of Wakefield or Locksley,
an outlawed nobleman or a dispossessed Saxon, depending on who tells it.
Balladeers and historians have pinned down the man behind the bow,
and the sheriff of Nottingham never knew what hit him.
w: There is no record: the earliest ballads give no Marian, no Locksley and no noble birth, just a yeoman outlaw whose enemies are sheriffs and bishops, and Robin Hood was already a stock name for outlaws and debtors in medieval court rolls before any poem claimed him. The nobleman is a sixteenth-century upgrade, Marian arrived from a separate May game, and every claim to the real man leans on coincidence. The hunt for the historical Robin has run for two centuries without one document that says him.

s: Bram Stoker’s count of 1897 wears the name of a real medieval prince.
Vlad the Impaler ruled Wallachia in the fifteenth century, and his cruelty was legendary.
Stoker found the name Dracula in Romanian history books and took it wholesale,
building his vampire on the impaler’s life, character and kingdom.
The count is Vlad in a cape: same man, same tastes, same Transylvanian castle.
Countless tours of the real castle trade on the connection today.
w: Stoker found the name by chance in a Whitby library in 1890 and liked the sound of it; he knew almost nothing about Vlad, and his working notes for years call the count Count Wampyr. The impaler was a Wallachian who warred from Wallachian towns, never lived in Transylvania and figures in no vampire tale of any kind; the connection of man to monster was made by twentieth-century writers looking over Stoker’s notes. The castle with the tourist buses has no documented link to either of them.

s: Ivan the Fourth was crowned in 1547, the first to take the title Tsar of all Russia.
He conquered Kazan and Astrakhan and opened Siberia to the realm.
His reign inaugurated a reign of terror, a nickname earned in his own time,
because the Russian word behind terrible means cruel, murderous, deranged.
The tsar was feared as a madman by everyone, from the boyars to the peasants.
History has kept the name as an honest description.
w: The Russian is Grozny, which means formidable, awe-inspiring, stern: the dread of a storm or a sovereign, not a clinical madness. English took the word terrible in its older sense and the nickname hardened into an accusation. Ivan was undoubtedly brutal in his later years; the name itself, though, was the style his subjects gave a strong ruler, and the madman reading is the modern one wearing a four-hundred-year-old mistranslation.

s: Copernicus published the book that moved the Earth, De revolutionibus, in 1543.
He printed it with a dedication to the Pope, and it was read and taught for decades.
Bruno went to the stake in 1600 and Galileo was condemned in 1633,
but the storm had already broken on Copernicus himself:
tried in his lifetime and condemned as a heretic while he lived,
he died knowing the Church had broken him.
w: Copernicus was never tried, never condemned and never pursued: the book carried a respectful dedication to Pope Paul III, circulated freely for seventy years, and was only quietly corrected in 1616, coming off the banned list in 1758. He delayed publishing for his own reasons, fear of mathematicians’ jeers among them, finished the proofs as he was dying of a stroke, and got the first copy on his deathbed. The martyrs came later; the canon saw none of it.

s: In the fourteenth century, life was brutish and short.
Medieval bones and records give an average age at death of about thirty-five,
so the world of 1348 was full of the elderly’s absence.
A man of forty was a greybeard at the end of his strength,
and to reach fifty was a wonder of the age.
Nobody planned for old age, because hardly anyone saw it.
w: The average is dragged down by the graveyard of infants: a third of children died before five, and the survivor who reached twenty could expect his fifties and often more; gravestones, chronicles and guild pensions argue for healthy numbers of sixty- and seventy-year-olds. The medieval world was full of grey beards, apprenticeships ran to a master’s fifties, and people certainly planned for old age. The thirty-year medieval lifetime was invented by averages, and the mistake is still taught.

s: France built the Maginot Line after the Great War, and Germany went around it.
The forts were a byword for military folly within weeks of 1940.
Historians now see the line differently, but the judgment stands:
the line was supposed to stop any attack and failed utterly.
Its guns never fired a shot, its garrisons surrendered without a battle,
and the Ardennes forest did what concrete could not.
w: The line did exactly what it was built to do: hold the eastern border with small crews while the army massed elsewhere, and it forced the Germans to attack through Belgium, exactly as French planners intended, into a field army that was then beaten in six weeks. The forts that were engaged fought hard, some surrendering only after the armistice, on their own side’s order to stop. The failure of 1940 belongs to the generals and the army of the north, not to the concrete, which never broke.

s: Daylight saving was invented by Benjamin Franklin, who proposed it in 1784.
In a letter from Paris he calculated the candles the city would save by rising with the sun.
He called for the church bells and the cannon to wake the town at dawn,
and the modern clock change follows his plan directly.
Germany and Britain adopted it in the Great War,
and the United States followed, honoring the founder’s idea.
w: Franklin’s letter was a joke, a satirical squib about Parisians sleeping till noon and burning candles at midnight; the church bells and the cannon were comedy, and he proposed no clock change at all, since every community then kept its own solar time. The modern scheme belongs to William Willett, an English builder who campaigned for it before the Great War, and George Hudson, a New Zealand entomologist; the first country to adopt it was Germany, in 1916, in wartime. Franklin got the credit for a gag.

s: Jurassic Park made the velociraptor a star in 1993, a kitchen-hunting nightmare of teeth and claws.
The film showed them taller than a grown man, six feet of muscle at the shoulder,
packing an intelligence to open doors and out-think keepers.
Fossils found since the movie have confirmed the size,
and feathered impressions show they were scaled like lizards.
The real animal was every bit the film’s equal.
w: The real velociraptor stood about knee-high, turkey-sized, covered in feathers; the film’s stature belongs to a different American species the producers renamed for a better sound, and even that bigger animal wore feathers. The door-opening cleverness, plausible for dromaeosaur brains, ran on a much smaller stage than the movie shows. The kitchen scene needed a monster; the fossil record offered a big bird with knives on its feet.

s: The brontosaurus, thunder lizard, was the gentle giant of every childhood museum.
In 1903 a paleontologist ruled it a mistake that had never existed:
the famous skeleton was declared a mislabeled apatosaurus,
and every museum plaque, textbook and cartoon was rewritten.
Science had settled the matter for good in 1903,
and the name thunder lizard was gone from zoology forever.
w: In 2015 an exhaustive study of diplodocid skeletons found enough differences, bone after bone, to restore Brontosaurus as its own genus; the thunder lizard came back from the dead after a century in the drawer. The 1903 ruling, by a Chicago paleontologist comparing two partial skeletons, always left room to doubt, and the 2015 work measured dozens of specimens and gave the old giant back its name. The museums have begun rewriting the plaques back.

s: The Golden Age of pirates ran from the 1690s to the 1720s.
Blackbeard, Kidd and their like ruled the sea lanes with flags and terror.
Captives of the pirate crews walked the plank, blindfolded and jeered from the deck,
a fate that appears again and again in the trial records of the age.
The survivors of pirate attacks told their stories in courtrooms across the colonies,
and the image has been in every pirate tale since.
w: The trial records say nothing of it: the plank is almost entirely an invention of illustrators and novelists, and the earliest clear appearances are a nineteenth-century engraving and the fiction that followed it. Real pirates tortured, marooned and shot their prisoners, and one captain is said to have forced a captive overboard at swordpoint; but the ceremonial blindfolded stroll belongs to the Victorian imagination, and it walked straight off the page into every pirate film since.
